title: The Rose and the Amaranth
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Rose and an Amaranth blossomed side by side in a garden, and the Amaranth said to her neighbour, "How I envy you your beauty and your sweet scent! No wonder you are such a universal favourite." But the Rose replied with a shade of sadness in her voice, "Ah, my dear friend, I bloom but for a time: my petals soon wither and fall, and then I die. But your flowers never fade, even if they are cut; for they are everlasting."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where do the Rose and the Amaranth blossom?
options: On opposite ends of a large field
In separate pots on a windowsill
Side by side in a garden
Along a path leading into a forest

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Amaranth envy about the Rose?
options: Her beauty and her sweet scent
Her ability to grow taller
Her resistance to insects
Her deep red color

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Amaranth call the Rose?
options: The rarest flower in the garden
A dangerous plant to touch
The oldest flower in the garden
A universal favourite

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Rose say happens to her petals?
options: They grow more fragrant with time
They soon wither and fall, and then she dies
They never change no matter the season
They are picked and sold at market each year

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Rose say about the Amaranth's flowers?
options: They fade just as quickly as her own petals do
They only bloom once every few years
They never fade, even if they are cut, for they are everlasting
They lose their scent after being cut

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Rose reply with "a shade of sadness" rather than pride?
options: She recognizes that her admired beauty comes at the cost of a short life
She is embarrassed that the Amaranth noticed her scent
She wishes she smelled like the Amaranth instead
She is upset that the Amaranth is envious of her

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what trade-off does the Rose point out between the two flowers?
options: The Amaranth is actually more beautiful than the Rose in every way
Both flowers share exactly the same lifespan and qualities
The Rose believes the Amaranth's flowers are ultimately worthless
Striking, admired beauty in her case comes with a brief life, while plain endurance in the Amaranth's case lasts far longer

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "everlasting" mean in "they are everlasting"?
options: Blooming only once a year
Lasting forever, without fading
Growing larger over time
Changing color with the seasons

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "wither" mean in "my petals soon wither and fall"?
options: To grow larger and fuller
To change to a brighter color
To dry up and shrink
To spread out and multiply

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Beauty that is brief and lasting endurance are two different kinds of value, each with its own cost
Everlasting flowers are always better than beautiful ones
Being admired by others is more important than living a long life
Envy between two things of equal worth is always misplaced

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Amaranth address the Rose?
options: As her rival
As her teacher
As a stranger
As her neighbour

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Rose call the Amaranth when she replies?
options: "My rival"
"My dear friend"
"My teacher"
"My envious neighbour"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Amaranth's flowers even if they are cut?
options: They wilt within a day
They change color slightly
They never fade
They lose their scent immediately

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Amaranth's envy of the Rose seem misplaced by the end of the passage?
options: The very quality she envies is tied to a short life the Amaranth does not have to face
The Amaranth actually has a sweeter scent than the Rose
The Rose admits she was never truly admired at all
The Amaranth's flowers are shown to fade just as quickly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Rose seem to value about the Amaranth's lack of fragrance and showy beauty?
options: Its ability to attract more admirers than her own petals do
Its ability to grow taller than any rose
Its ability to change color throughout the year
Its ability to endure, which her own beauty cannot match

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "universal favourite" mean in "such a universal favourite"?
options: Someone chosen at random from a group
Someone or something admired by nearly everyone
Someone who dislikes being noticed
Someone rarely seen in public

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Rose envies the Amaranth's everlasting flowers and wishes to trade places
The Rose and Amaranth agree they are equally beautiful and long-lasting
An Amaranth envies the Rose's beauty, but the Rose points out that her beauty is brief while the Amaranth's plainer flowers last forever
The Amaranth withers first, proving the Rose's claim wrong
